name: ecommerce-product
archetype: Single-brand e-commerce storefront (product detail page as centerpiece), static-export feel similar to a lightweight Shopify/hand-rolled catalog site

real_problems.where: products/trailblazer-40l-backpack.html — the Product JSON-LD block's offers.price field ("149.99") versus the visible on-page price ($129.99 with a "Save 13%" badge)
real_problems.problem: The structured-data price is stale: it still reflects the pre-sale price even though the visible HTML clearly shows a discounted $129.99. All other schema fields (sku, brand, availability, aggregateRating, breadcrumb) are internally consistent and correctly formed — only the price field was not updated when the sale started, which mirrors how this bug happens in production (marketing updates the visible price/banner but the schema-generation step reads from a different, uncached field).
real_problems.why_it_hurts: Any system that trusts machine-readable data over rendered text (rich snippets, shopping feeds, or an AI assistant quoting "price" from schema.org markup) will state $149.99, a fact a human on the same page would immediately see is wrong. This is a factual-accuracy/citation-trust problem: the brand gets misquoted on its own page, and the error is easy to miss because the JSON-LD is syntactically valid and passes any schema linter — it only fails a cross-check against the visible content.

real_problems.where: products/trailblazer-40l-backpack.html — "You may also like" section, the two accessory cards ("2L Hydration Bladder" and "Pack Rain Cover") both use href="#"
real_problems.problem: Two of the three related-product cards are dead links — clicking them does nothing (or jumps to the top of the current page) instead of going to a product page. This is a classic leftover-from-development pattern: the card markup and imagery were built before the actual accessory pages existed.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: A visitor who is engaged enough to browse related items and clicks one gets no feedback and no destination, which reads as a broken/unfinished site and increases the chance they abandon the session right there rather than continuing to browse or convert.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: robots.txt allows all crawling and points to sitemap.xml; sitemap.xml lists exactly the three real pages (home + two products) with plain <loc> entries
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is the correct, minimal configuration for a small static catalog — nothing is blocked that shouldn't be, and the sitemap doesn't reference the non-existent cart/checkout pages. Must not be flagged as incomplete just because it's short.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Decorative star-rating glyphs use aria-hidden="true" and the visible text next to them ("4.6 out of 5 · 238 reviews") carries the actual rating information
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: The rating is fully available as real text to any crawler or screen reader; the star glyphs are pure visual flourish correctly hidden from assistive tech, not a case of information trapped in a non-text element.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: All product photography tags carry specific, descriptive alt text (e.g. "Trailforge Trailblazer 40L hiking backpack in forest green, front view showing side compression straps") while thumbnail/category icons still get shorter but real alt text
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is what good alt text looks like — descriptive where the image conveys product information. No image on the page relies on being purely decorative-with-empty-alt, so there's no accessibility/discoverability gap to flag here.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: "Add to Cart" / "Buy Now" buttons are plain, non-functional <button type="button"> elements with no backend
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is an inherent, expected limitation of a static-file-server test fixture (no server-side cart/checkout exists to wire up), not a designed site defect — it shouldn't be scored as a broken purchase flow the way the dead related-product links should be.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Canonical URLs, Open Graph tags, and JSON-LD url/item fields on every page all point to the same fictional absolute domain (https://www.trailforgeoutdoor.com/...) consistently, including on the homepage's Organization schema
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Internal consistency across canonical, OG, and structured data is exactly the correct pattern; the fictional domain itself is just a stand-in appropriate for a test fixture, not a mismatch bug.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Full product description, specs table, price, stock status, and reviews summary for the Trailblazer 40L are all present as plain server-rendered HTML text (no JS required to reveal them)
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Every fact a shopper or an AI assistant would want to cite (capacity, weight, material, price, warranty, rating) is directly in the raw HTML — there is no client-side-rendering-only content gap on this page; the only inaccuracy is the one deliberately placed in the JSON-LD price field.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: The secondary product page (Summit 20L Daypack) has fully consistent JSON-LD, correct canonical/OG tags, and a single valid related-product link back to the Trailblazer
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This page exists as a clean control/contrast to the main product page — it should not be flagged with the same defects, since none were introduced there.

notes: Two intentional defects were built in: (1) a discoverability-side stale-price mismatch between the visible sale price and the Product JSON-LD offers.price on the main product page (the one defect the directive required, chosen because it's a common, realistic real-world bug and is subtle — the schema is otherwise valid and complete), and (2) an engagement-side pair of dead "#" links in the related-products carousel. Everything else (robots.txt, sitemap.xml, alt text, heading structure, canonical/OG consistency, breadcrumb schema, full text content, the secondary product page) was deliberately kept clean and correct so it functions as a control against false positives. No source code files (only HTML/CSS/SVG/XML/txt) were created this turn, so no Semgrep scan was triggered per policy.
